item.title: [AINews] Riemann Hypothesis proved...twice independently
item.abstract: Within a few hours of each other ( timeline ), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics ( Scientific American ). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human , work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett ). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible , and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable . Open models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Code, at the lowest cost per fix. As Levent eloquently put it: “ Claude far outpaced me near the finish line . No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” This also ties into other AI themes we’ve covered on the podcast and on this newsletter: The nature of Slop : Levent says “ I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics. It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of "slop", I decided to only present Lean . ” One of the key tenets of the No Slop Manifesto is that you should understand what you ship (“ Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it. ”). And yet, this giant pile of Lean is verifiably correct and is incredibly significant in human history. Should we have delayed its release by a decade simply because we didn’t understand every single bit of it? Weak to Strong alignment : the typical experience of using agents is Strong to Weak - we are general intelligences guiding not-as-smart AI to do things we know how to do well. We also often expect AI to automate most work “within distribution”, and expect it to run into more trouble at the limits of capability where the “centaur” pattern of human-AI-collaboration is required. Levent’s lived experience is the opposite - collaborating with Claude only in the early stages and then leaving him far behind with the critical parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups. We are starting to need Weak to Strong alignment — the open ended domain of controlling AI smarter than us. If your data is growing faster than planned, you need storage that grows with your business, feeds flash and GPUs with terabit-scale throughput, and doesn’t charge egress. Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies. Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building. Claimed Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude The claim : Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says that, "working with Claude," he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. He says the method also covers the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) ( Scientific American , statement summary , remark.pdf link ). Artifact : Only Lean code was released. A written-out prose version reportedly ran past 250,000 pages ( timeline ). Timeline : The work began on Oct 6. Eight of the 20 steps landed on Nov 15, and the final entry on Nov 16 reads "GRH." Alpöge credits Claude for the parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups, an area where he says he has little mastery ( breakdown ). Unknowns : The Claude model used and the degree of human steering have not been disclosed ( open questions ). Verification status : Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH. The Lean code is "still compiling, will take a few hours." He puts the chance of a Lean bug at <<1% ( analysis ). Provisional status : Artificial Analysis notes that both AI-claimed Millennium results are unverified: this one and OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim, which used an unreleased model ( tally ). Competing human proof : Alessandro Masullo has announced a separate, purely human proof of RH. It is reported as a roughly 940-page GRH draft ( announcement , page count ). Interpretation debate : Some argue the result shows we have little idea how hard math problems objectively are, rather than showing broad superhuman ability ( Theo Jaffee , Ege Erdil ). Brute-force framing : Others compare the approach to olympiad-style "bashing" at a scale humans lack the willpower for ( cloneofsimo ). Jaggedness : Omar Khattab notes the contrast between solving Millennium problems and being "this dumb on 1000 other things" ( post ). Market reaction : ANT stock fell about 10% on the day ( scaling01 , Nabeel Qureshi ). Unconfirmed rumor : A DeepMind "math horizon" repo appearing the same day prompted speculation about Gemini math results ( unconfirmed ). Thinking Machines Releases Inkling 2 Mini, an Open-Weights Looped Transformer Inkling 2 Mini : A 26.4B-parameter looped MoE under Apache 2.0, pitched as small enough for a laptop. It scores 20.1 on the AA Index ( launch , Mira Murati ). Architecture : There are 12 shared core layers run for 3 passes, with gated messages carried between passes ( vLLM ). Active parameters : 3.4B unique active parameters, or 5.4B effective counting the loops. It has a 1M context window and accepts text and image input ( AA ). Training recipe : Two-thirds of the experts were pruned during mid-training, followed by logit distillation from a larger Inkling ( eliebakouch ). Claimed results : It leads open models under 100B on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%) ( via teortaxes ). Comparison to Inkling 1.0 : It reportedly beats Inkling 1.0 at 2.7% of the size ( Ziqiao Ma ). Vals : It ties Claude Opus 5.5 on CyberBench at under a quarter of the cost and keeps 96–97% of Inkling 2 Small's Vibe Code and SAGE scores ( Vals , details ). Artificial Analysis : AA places it on the Pareto frontier for intelligence vs. active parameters ( AA ). ARC-AGI-2 : It reportedly scores 49.3% at $0.14/task, well below Inkling 2 Small ( teortaxes ). Safety and interpretability rationale : Thinking Machines says the open release is meant to let researchers study how loops affect chain-of-thought monitorability ( Alex Robey ). Variable-loop model : A companion research model, TML-d24-varloop-research, shows long-context scores (GraphWalks, MRCR v2) improving with more passes. Knowledge benchmarks such as SimpleQA and AA-Omniscience do not improve ( Ziqiao Ma ). Goodfire analysis : Goodfire mapped information flow across layers, blocks and loops ( Goodfire ). NDIF hosting : NDIF hosts both models with tooling for activation patching across loops ( NDIF ). Serving and local availability : vLLM had day-0 support. GB200 decode : TP1 decode on GB200 drops from 10.29 to 3.84 ms at batch 1, with kernels per step falling from 4,278 to 927 ( numbers ). Local runtimes : Ollama 0.40.17-rc3 ( Ollama ), Unsloth GGUF quants targeting 16GB RAM ( Unsloth ), transformers, llama.cpp and MLX ( HF ).

item.title: Meet Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Mini: 26B Looped MoE Runs on a 32GB Mac
item.abstract: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini , an open-weight looped transformer with 26.4B total parameters. The model reuses its middle layers 3 times per token instead of adding more weights. That keeps the checkpoint near 20GB, small enough for a 32GB Mac or 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark. For developers, Inkling 2 Mini is a local option for agentic coding, tool use and document work. It ships under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face , with hosted inference and fine-tuning on Tinker . Inkling 2 Mini is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from Thinking Machines that loops its middle layers. It accepts text and images and returns text only. It follows Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter model released on November 5. The model stores 24 layers, grouped into 4 blocks of 6. The first and last blocks run once. The 2 middle blocks run 3 times with shared weights. That gives 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights. Each pass after the first receives a “message” from the previous pass. Thinking Machines carries it with Attention Residuals and a learned gate. Feed-forward layers use 128 experts, with 8 routed per token. Looping the middle layers gave a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain. Looping the last layers gave only 1.24x to 1.36x. The middle-loop variant won 27 of 28 evaluations. Looping costs training compute but saves inference. An unlooped baseline used 7.5% less training compute. It needed 140% more inference compute to match the looped model’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces. Training began with 384 experts per layer, with 8 active per token. At midtraining, the team pruned two-thirds of them and kept the 128 most-used experts. A 1T-token distillation run from a larger internal Inkling model then healed the pruned model. Post-training used SFT, then RL over 2.2T tokens and 2,000 steps, plus on-policy distillation. Expert layers are trained and deployed in NVFP4. The last 4 layers use MXFP8. Thinking Machines says this removes quantization conversion loss. A research variant, TML-d24-varloop-research , trains with 1 to 5 passes. All Inkling scores below are self-reported by Thinking Machines. Coding is the strongest area. Inkling 2 Mini scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only) and 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 (Hard). It reaches 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, where Qwen’s own card lists Qwen3.8-27B at 42.2%. On Terminal Bench v2.1 it scores 71.6%, behind Qwen3.8-27B at 73.0%. Agentic search also holds up: 79.0% on BrowseComp with compaction and 82.7% on MCP Atlas. For documents and vision, it posts 92.8% on OmniDocBench v1.6 and 74.9% on MMMU Pro. On reasoning, it scores 86.6% on GPQA Diamond and 49.3% on ARC-AGI-2. Efficiency is the headline claim. On Stanford’s Intelligence per Watt metric, Thinking Machines reports 0.703 on a DGX Spark. It lists Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 0.430 and Gemma-4-26B-A4B at 0.159. Each column uses the vendor’s own model card. Harnesses and settings differ, so treat cross-vendor gaps as directional. The checkpoint is about 20GB in Safetensors. Thinking Machines lists 3 supported setups: 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark, Apple silicon with 32GB+ memory, and other GPUs with 32GB+ VRAM. Quantized GGUF builds are available through Unsloth and llama.cpp. Serving support covers Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, NVIDIA Dynamo and TokenSpeed. Tinker pricing for Mini is not disclosed in the launch materials. A vLLM quick start takes 1 command: vllm serve "thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini" . Knowledge depends mostly on total parameters, and looping did not help knowledge benchmarks. Inkling 2 Mini scores -8.6 on AA-Omniscience, with a 63.4% non-hallucination rate. It is not the best small model for multi-turn chat or constraint-heavy prompts. It scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1. It also trails larger models on HLE-Diamond (15.2%) and CritPt v2. Check out the technical blog , model card , model weights and Tinker Playground . item.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
item.abstract:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

(686 points, 547 comments on Hacker News)

item.title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
item.abstract: Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache ” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks. This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro , Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer. The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything: These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following: We gave the agent this prompt: “My vLLM fleet serves a legal assistant with 64K-token contexts on p5 instances. Returning conversations take 13 seconds for the first token because the GPU recomputes the full conversation history every turn. How do I fix this?” The agent matches the request to the skill and, in Kiro, asks for approval before loading it. The answer identifies that the latency was caused by cold prefill, and three things in the answer matter for a real deployment. First, it checks for fixes that need no new infrastructure. If you turned off prefix caching, turning it back on can speed up back-to-back turns. If the GPU prefix cache hit rate is already above 90% with session affinity, you might not need a shared KV cache. Second, it identifies constraints specific to the legal AI assistant. A shared KV cache can let one tenant tell from response times whether another tenant sent the same text. Cases that must stay isolated get separate caches, and tenants that share a cache add their own ID to the KV hash. Third, it doesn’t guess the size. It asks for the model and TP size, KV data type, replica count and routing, and how long users wait between turns. Figure 1: The diagnosis and proposed architecture for the legal assistant To size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant. The agent looked up the GPU and cache node prices and derived the prefill rate and KV size from benchmarks. Finally, the agent recommended two cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes for distributed KV caching. The following figure shows the agent’s summary and the inputs it used. Figure 2: The agent’s summary and inputs. It looked up both prices in the AWS price list and explains how it arrived at the recompute figure We didn’t provide a cache hit rate, which is the share of recomputed tokens the cache would serve. The agent therefore presents scenarios and recommends a KVTrace run to identify the cache hit rate. KVTrace records the KV cache events from vLLM or SGLang. It then replays them offline against a shared KV cache of each candidate size. The recorder never writes token IDs or prompt text. Traces hold block hashes and token counts. Block hashes come from token content, so pass --anonymize-key-file when your prompts are sensitive. The skill records on every GPU server for a representative window, such as a full business day. The agent also notes that freed GPU time turns into dollars only if you run fewer servers or serve more traffic on the same ones. Figure 3: The top of a KVTrace report from synthetic demo traffic. It recommends the smallest capacity that reaches 90% of the savings ceiling. We prompted the agent with: “Set up a shared L2 KV cache for LLM inference, starting from scratch.” Before it creates anything, the agent requests your confirmation to set up the suggested cache node count in your Availability Zone, at the estimated price. Once confirmed, it creates the right security group with EFA permissions, and a Valkey 9.1 cluster that uses a custom parameter group with caching eviction policies. LMCache gets its own cache user , with the password in AWS Secrets Manager . The agent prepares the GPU servers and starts one LMCache server per GPU server. Then it checks the cluster with a small test object and confirms that repeated prompts load their KV state from the cache over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). On a GPU fleet, the skill checks the measured L2 share against the KVTrace prediction. For the full setup with every command, see Getting started with distributed KV caching in the Amazon ElastiCache documentation. Prompt: “My LMCache server connects to the ElastiCache cluster and BLOB.RDMA_HELLO succeeds, but actual data transfers are failing. INFO largeobj shows rdma_write_errors climbing. What’s wrong?” Following the skill’s troubleshooting guide, the agent reasons from the symptom pattern and identifies the likely cause as a security group that blocks EFA traffic between its own members. It provides you commands to check and fix the rule. Figure 4: The agent explains the symptom, then gives commands to check and fix the security group You can get the distributed KV caching skill or the AWS MCP Server from the Agent Toolkit for AWS . Then describe your problem or ask your AI agent to cut costs and latency on your GPU fleet to get started. To learn more about distributed KV caching with ElastiCache and the performance benchmarks see the AWS blog . You can see getting started with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) at Amazon ElastiCache documentation and learn more about KVTrace at the GitHub repo .

item.title: Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index
item.abstract: Baseten has released bison-1 and groundhog-1, 2 open-weight decision models built on Google’s Gemma 4 . Decision models do not write text. They return calibrated probabilities for yes/no, choice and score questions. The Baseten bison-1 decision model scores 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 . That ranks #1 of 19. Both models raise context from 16k to 128k tokens and accept images. For routing, triage and guardrail pipelines, that means full policies and histories in one call. bison-1 is a 31B decision model from Baseten that post-trains Gemma 4 31B to return calibrated probabilities. groundhog-1 is the cheaper sibling. It fine-tunes Gemma 4 26B-A4B , a mixture-of-experts model with about 4B active parameters per token. Both join Baseten’s existing lineup: mammoth-1 (27B), elephant-1 (9B) and joey-1 (2B). Those 3 sit on Qwen backbones. The new pair is Baseten’s first on what it calls an American backbone. A request carries 1 state and any number of questions . The state is text, optionally with images. Each question has a type: noul (yes/no), choice (named options) or score (ordered levels). The model answers every question in a single prefill pass. It returns P(yes), or the chosen option with a probabilities field. No output tokens are generated. Baseten’s earlier launch post lists ticket triage, spam detection, jailbreak guardrails and LLM routing as target tasks. Requests longer than the trained limit are refused, not truncated. Pipelines that assume silent truncation will need a length check. Baseten credits two sources: the Gemma base and more “soft labels” in the training mix. Soft labels use probability targets instead of 1 fixed correct answer. The model learns to report uncertainty that tracks how often it is right. The result is a Brier score of 0.14, the lowest on the index. Baseten puts d1.2-ultra at 0.15. Lower is better. On AA Decision Index v2.1, bison-1 scores 76. Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra scores 75 and mammoth-1 scores 71. The index blends 6 evaluations, led by AA-Paperclip at 30%. The bison-1 model card breaks out each component: bison-1 ranks first on 4 of 6 components. Knowledge-heavy decisions are its weak spot. On long context, Baseten reports LongMemEval M (128k) of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1. LongMemEval S reads 87.1 and 79.3. groundhog-1 has no official index score yet. Baseten expects it to match mammoth-1. Both models are live on Baseten Model APIs . They use the same API as the older decision models, so switching means changing 1 model name. The IDs are decision-models/baseten-bison-latest and decision-models/baseten-groundhog-latest . Pricing mirrors the older pair. bison-1 costs $0.10 per 1M tokens, like mammoth-1. groundhog-1 costs $0.035, like elephant-1. The bison-1 library page lists that as an input price, since no output tokens are produced. Open BF16 weights sit on Hugging Face. Baseten lists no inference GPU or quantized builds. Training used 192 B200 GPUs for bison-1 and 128 for groundhog-1. Check out the launch post , the bison-1 and groundhog-1 model cards, and the Baseten docs . item.title: How Public Evals Work and Fail, and What Should Change
item.abstract: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. Patterns: How eval tasks are built and maintained # Most eval tasks share four components: Instruction: A prompt that sounds like a real user’s request. The agent gets it once at the start and typically can’t ask clarifying questions. Environment: The workspace where the agent operates. Typically comes with the files, software, and services needed. For coding, this is usually a container with a repo at a specific git commit. For knowledge work, it might be a VM with installed software, simulated business apps, or a folder of documents. Grader: This decides whether the work passes. It can be deterministic code (tests and assertions over the final output or environment state), an LLM judge scoring a rubric of yes/no criteria, or a mix of both. Reference (optional): A human expert’s solution. Evals include this to prove a task is solvable, anchor pairwise comparisons, or establish a human baseline. The four basic components of an eval task In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Principles: That shape grading and task selection # Across the benchmarks studied, four design principles show up repeatedly: Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% useful . Nonetheless, all-pass can be brittle where a single flawed assertion or criterion fails an otherwise correct solution. One alternative is partial credit, where each test or criterion carries a weight and tasks score from 0.0 to 1.0. FrontierSWE and HealthBench Professional use partial credit, while Agents’ Last Exam, Finance Agent, and OSWorld 2.0 report both. Tasks are mined for difficulty to slow saturation. AutomationBench hardened easy tasks with irrelevant data and conflicting policies. HealthBench Professional made difficult tasks about 3.5x more common (than in the base set). BrowseComp kept a question only if the strongest models at the time couldn’t solve it, and Terminal Bench retires tasks once they saturate. Failures: Skipped verification and dropped reqs # Across the error analyses, two failure modes come up repeatedly: Skipping verification or stopping early. On OSWorld 2.0, agents submitted their work without checking the final state. On Harvey LAB, agents that drafted without review scored lower. And on AutomationBench, models processed part of a list, summarized as if they’d finished, and incorrectly declared success. Missing stated requirements. Instruction following was the most common failure in GDPval, and agents on OSWorld 2.0 dropped constraints explicitly stated in the prompt. Many of these misses are unforced errors that a basic verification pass should have caught. Gaps: Failing correct work and passing wrong work # Not every failure is the model’s fault. Many evals have two recurring grader gaps. False negatives (failing correct work). This is the most common issue, usually caused by a check that’s stricter than what the prompt requested, or enforces an unstated requirement. Reviewers found that 41 of 65 Terminal Bench 4.0 tasks were graded on unstated requirements, and that 23 of 113 DeepSWE tasks marked correct solutions as failures. On OSWorld 2.0, an outside reviewer filed issues reporting checks that failed correct work in 23 of 108 tasks, such as a grader whose software can’t open the task’s own starter file . This is amplified under all-pass scoring where a single flawed check can cause an entire task to fail. False negatives can also come from wrong or ambiguous answer keys, where the reference answer or criterion is wrong or isn’t unique. On BrowseComp, human trainers who solved a question disagreed with the reference answer on 50 of 367 questions (14%). A later paper confirmed errors in 10 of 200 sampled questions from BrowseComp-Plus (which reuses BrowseComp’s questions). Harvey LAB removed 17 (unsolvable) criteria from the held-out set and a contributor reported that they couldn’t find the requested damages estimate in any of the source documents. False positives (passing wrong work). Assertions and rubric items usually check that an expected point is present, not that the rest of the work is correct. On Harvey LAB, Artificial Analysis used an LLM judge to check deliverables against the source documents, and found material hallucinations in more than 60% of the results that passed every criterion . On AutomationBench, 55% of the assertions only check whether a message or record contains or excludes a string, leaving room for an agent to match the keyword while getting the rest wrong. For example, one task asks for an email with the counts of ready and not-ready audit items, and checks only that the email contains a “3” and a “4” —any email that swaps the two counts would pass. Hot takes: How we’re thinking about evals wrongly # Looking ahead, here’s where I believe our thinking on evals is off, and what should change. Some of these are based on the benchmarks studied while others are vibes. We should measure reliability ( pass k \text{pass}^k ) in addition to the average pass rate. Most evals report average pass rate—this hides a huge difference in production. Consider two agents that both score 70%. The first solves 70% of tasks every time, while the second solves every task 70% of the time. We can trust the first on the 70% of tasks it’s reliable on, but have to check every output from the second. pass k \text{pass}^k (popularized by τ \tau -bench ) distinguishes them by counting a task as solved only if the agent passes all k k trials. Over five trials, the first still scores 70% while the second falls to 17%.

為什麼不基於DeepSeek harness開發🤣跟ds-bot有何區別呢 對此，Tony Zhang回應道： Linger的重點是把模型和harness一起最佳化：12GB顯示卡就能本地跑125B模型，不按token付費，資料也不出本機。 從產品定位上看：DS-Bot的核心是Bot與Bot、Bot與群組的協作；Linger的核心是人與自己的Agent、Agent與本地環境。 item.title: 米哈遊發了個VLA論文
item.abstract: 米哈遊發了個VLA論文 衡宇 2026-11-21 00:25:26 來源： 量子位 8B參數，50小時自主執行 henry 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 米哈遊，您是準備親自下場研究“官方指令碼”了？ （doge） 就在米哈遊崩壞AI研發團隊最新發布的研究 Gamer 中—— 你敢信，AI竟然自己玩起了《崩壞：星穹鐵道》。 鍵盤滑鼠交給AI，上來就能和可可利亞打上一架。 碰上場景機關，也能自己上手。走到“氣泡彈珠”前啟動裝置，把自己彈到另一片區域，落地接著跑。 跟著NPC跑圖同樣可以，流螢在前面帶路，AI就在後面跟著，上樓梯、拐彎，一路跑到廣場。 我勒個乖乖，這打Boss、開機關、跟人跑圖，都讓AI學會了。 這以後充值頁面裡，會不會有個“AI代肝”選項？ （注：《崩壞：星穹鐵道》是米哈遊開發的一款銀河冒險題材的回合制角色扮演遊戲。玩家乘坐星穹列車探索不同世界，通過跑圖、對話和解謎推進劇情，並組建角色隊伍進行回合制戰鬥。） VLA代肝，不燒心 咱言歸正傳，米哈遊給Gamer的定位，是面向長流程、即時互動的 通用視覺—語言—動作 （VLA） 基礎模型。 上面演示玩《崩鐵》的主力版本，由團隊基於參數量80億的 Qwen3-VL-8B 進一步訓練而來。 它能根據遊戲畫面和任務，決定按哪些鍵、滑鼠往哪裡移動、什麼時候點選，再把這些操作真正執行出來。 換句話說，螢幕畫面是它接收的視覺訊號，任務指令告訴它要做什麼，鍵鼠操作則是它輸出的動作。 相較於以往的AI玩遊戲，Gamer這次最大的亮點是 把跨遊戲的即時操作與長流程的記憶、規劃，接進同一套VLA框架。 實戰時，模型完全依靠螢幕畫面、任務指令和已有記憶做判斷， 無需讀取遊戲內部介面或底層狀態。 隨著任務推進，它還會動態記錄“剛才完成了什麼”、“下一步準備幹什麼”。 在論文中，研究還給出了一組硬核的實測資料：在覆蓋五個主線篇章、總計約50小時的《崩鐵》長流程評估中，Gamer的自主執行時間佔比超過了95%。 而為了實現這一效果，研究設計了一套三階段訓練流程： 先用跨遊戲資料練操作，再用任務示範補上思考和記憶，最後讓模型進入遊戲，通過試錯和反饋繼續提升。 首先，是持續預訓練 （Continued Pre-Training，CPT） ，讓已經具備圖文理解能力的基座模型，進一步學會操作遊戲。 具體來說，團隊把不同遊戲的錄屏與玩家操作對齊，讓模型學習畫面和動作之間的關係：人物往前走，場景會怎樣變化；滑鼠往右移，鏡頭會轉向哪裡。 這些操作被整理成統一的鍵鼠格式，讓不同遊戲的資料可以進入同一套訓練流程。 執行時，Gamer每隔200毫秒讀取一次畫面，一次安排隨後六個動作塊，每個約33毫秒，對應30Hz的控制節奏。 相當於看一眼，安排接下來一小段動作，再根據新畫面繼續調整。 其次，在微調階段，團隊整理了約1000小時高質量《崩鐵》演示，把目標分成具體操作、階段性小目標和完整任務，教模型將動作組織起來。 值得一提的是，這裡有兩個極其實用的工程設計，核心目的都是解決長流程中的推理延遲與上下文爆炸問題： – 稀疏思考”機制： 沿著確定的路線前進，可以直接操作；遇到路線失敗、目標切換或者新的互動提示，再展開推理。 – 記憶摘要機制： 舊記錄即將移出上下文時，模型先記下任務進度、失敗嘗試、重要地點和後續計劃，讓接下來的操作有據可循。 -“稀疏思考”：沿著確定的路線前進，可以直接操作；遇到路線失敗、目標切換或者新的互動提示，再展開推理。 最後，在線上強化學習階段，團隊提出TA-GRPO，把長流程拆成由記憶銜接的片段，比較不同嘗試在相應階段的表現，再利用遊戲環境核驗的結果更新模型。 比如，有沒有到達目標地點、有沒有完成當前任務，都能成為訓練反饋，訓練後臺則負責初始化和核驗。 此外，配套的 Streaming-vLLM 推理引擎還能複用已處理的上下文，並提前吐出生成且核驗完畢的動作塊，讓遊戲畫面先動起來，大幅壓低操作延遲。 實驗測試 在跨遊戲實驗中，團隊測試了Gamer的CPT版本，涵蓋《我的世界》、基於《毀滅戰士》的ViZDoom，以及OmniGameArena和GameWorld等多個遊戲環境。 比如在《我的世界》裡，它能自己轉視角鎖定史萊姆，追上去揮劍劈砍： 切到第一人稱射擊遊戲ViZDoom，它又能迅速拉槍瞄準，連續點射逼近的敵人： 此外，在上述四項公共基準上，Gamer-8B-CPT的平均得分為29.5，所列通用模型對照中，最高為僅17.6。 而在七類小遊戲、共40個未參與訓練的任務中，基座模型僅有 3.2%，經過CPT升至15.0%，SFT後提升至39.2%，加入強化學習後更是達到了49.7%—— 作為對比，同場競技的通用模型最高分 （GPT-6.1-Sol） 僅為 17.1%。 這些結果支援了團隊的核心判斷： 通過統一的鍵鼠介面，把跨遊戲學習、長期記憶和即時操作結合起來，可以讓AI在複雜遊戲中持續執行任務，並通過互動繼續改進。 團隊也在論文結尾指出，這類能力有望用於自動化測試、加快遊戲迭代，並支援新的玩法機制，從而降低開發成本。 遊戲成為AI的練習場，練出來的AI，又能反過來幫助開發遊戲。 團隊介紹 最後，我們來認識一下這項研究背後的團隊。 論文貢獻者名單共列出了8位共同一作，其中5位在米哈遊實習期間參與了該專案的研發： Run Luo： 新加坡國立大學電腦科學博士生，曾參與GUI-R1、OpenOmni等專案，在Gamer中負責三階段訓練、資料、基礎設施及評測建設。 張寬 （Kuan Zhang） ： 清華大學人工智慧學院博士生，GameScaling與GameVerse共同一作，主要負責持續預訓練、資料及評測建設。 item.title: OpenAI Ships GPT-Live-1.1 for Voice Agents, Cuts Idle Cost to $0.02/Min
item.abstract: OpenAI has made GPT-Live-1.1 available in its API under the model ID gpt-live-1.1 . The GPT-Live-1.1 voice model is a full-duplex model for multilingual conversations. It can listen while it speaks. OpenAI team states that it speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages and completes tasks more reliably. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions. For teams running voice agents, idle time on a call now costs less. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . GPT-Live-1.1 is a full-duplex speech model from OpenAI that hears and speaks in 1 stream. It follows GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026 . As per the OpenAI forum announcement , it has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. Inputs and outputs are audio and text. Image and video are not supported. Streaming and function calling work. Structured outputs, fine-tuning and predicted outputs do not. The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model . It also handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Deeper work is delegated. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model. OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks. Third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses . Responses mode uses OpenAI models. Client mode connects your own backend. Instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. OpenAI lists 4 improvement areas for 1.1: Standby pauses inference during silence while the WebRTC connection stays open. The guide documents 3 settings: After the timeout, the server emits session.paused . When the user speaks, session.resumed fires. The session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower. Keep the microphone track active during standby. Standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1. Voice sessions are billed by duration. The GPT-Live-1 model page says billing is per second. Backend model and tool usage are billed separately. That matters: a heavy backend can cost more than the voice layer. The model is API-only. You switch an existing Live session by setting model to gpt-live-1.1 . Changing the model requires a new session. Outbound SIP calling reached all organizations on November 2, so phone agents are supported. GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1 have separate concurrent-session limits. Each limit applies across inference regions. The 1.1 page does not publish tier numbers. Check out the model page , the Live conversations guide and the announcement . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol: The System Card
item.abstract: We have to stop meeting like this. Alas, we will keep meeting like this. It is time, once again, to do the reading . As per usual, I will focus on things to the extent they are new and important. There are a lot of things that need to be in the system card in case something goes wrong, but that look exactly the way you would expect. I did my best to skip those. I continue to be on vacation. I am aware that via Claude there is now a claimed Lean proof of the Reimann Hypothesis and will cover that next week. They start with the highlights. They have been using these models internally. They are using various controls for internal use, similar to those on external use. Okie dokie. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : Based on the assessment below, we determined that GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol meet the Critical threshold for Cybersecurity capabilities and the High threshold for Biological and Chemical capabilities. We determined that GPT-6.2 Astra meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement capabilities, while GPT-6.2 Sol does not reach the High threshold. GPT-6.2 Astra is therefore the first model we are deploying externally that meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement. As described in the Internal Deployment section above and the Safeguards section below, we have applied our strongest safeguards yet to GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. We have also strengthened our internal safety and security posture to address risks that might emerge from malicious misuse by human actors and from unauthorized, misaligned model behavior. High-level biological tests regressed slightly. There is net small progress on the Critical-level tests. I notice I am worried about eval awareness and potential sandbagging here, more because I worry about sandbagging generally than that I care about the scores. I doubt that the models deserve the Critical designation here, but I am not so confident that they don’t. If we were not already Critical in Cyber I would be more worried about this. If the results are accurate, there has been very little progress since GPT-6 Astra. There were several outside evaluations as well. My best fit to this data, given everything else we know, is that Astra sensed it was being evaluated and was less inclined to do well at these tasks, and is effectively sandbagging whether or not that was a conscious choice. We also see evidence of potential sandbagging in the answers to SecureBio, and in some work for UK AISI. We are already at Critical for Cybersecurity. Perhaps we should have a higher fifth level of risk on this to test for. We do not. It is still a good question how much cyber capabilities improved from 6 to 6.2. It is hard to interpret the tests but it reads as ‘a moderate amount additionally capable.’ They got external evaluations from UK AISI and Irregular. UK AISI places 6.2 Astra on the frontier for cyber. Irregular’s results do not show improvement from 6 Astra. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : GPT-6.2 Astra meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement capabilities, while GPT-6.2 Sol does not. They say ‘capabilities.’ Same thing. They edited the wording here on launch day from ‘this is coming’ to ‘this might someday happen.’ Again, close enough. This is only a ‘tracked category’ but these are the tests that matter for predicting and deciding how to act. We’re already going to guard against bio and cyber. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : That NanoGPT score is indicative of how quickly AI goes from ‘not that helpful’ to ‘very helpful’ on tasks once it gets good enough. This is a huge jump. I don’t think these tests are enough for a great picture. I do think that they are good enough if combined with a gestalt of experience from internal use. In general, I notice that I would like more curiosity around the places where scores regressed. Presumably you should have some idea why that happened. There are not that many data points. It is hard to say whether this is on trend, or whether it is above trend. The gap is very small between Sol and Astra here, despite a number of other tests showing substantial differences. Epoch’s version of the ECI, the original, found Fable 5.2 and 6.2 Astra neck and neck. Anthropic was previously trailing OpenAI on the ECI. Now that we are focusing on ECI as the metric, there is at least some chance that Anthropic’s trend line change is an artifact of them catching up on capabilities and resources and also shifting focus. Thus, we have the usual paradox, where we have a model that looks extremely impressive from some angles and disappointingly similar to past models from other angles. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model we are deploying externally that we determine meets the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement under our Preparedness Framework, in addition to the Critical threshold in Cybersecurity and High in Biological and Chemical capabilities. … Our safeguards for GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are designed to address both deliberate misuse by malicious actors and unauthorized actions by models during otherwise legitimate work. … We have also tightened access to more permissive configurations of GPT-6.2 Astra. Reduced cybersecurity refusals are planned to be available only to the smaller group separately approved for Daybreak Red at launch. Trusted access remains specific to the approved domain and use, with monitoring and restrictions on the highest-risk assistance continuing to apply. Alongside these misuse protections, we have expanded our misalignment monitoring and strengthened containment for internal training and evaluation. … We are also beginning to prepare for crossing our Critical threshold [in Bio]. We are developing four representative scenarios for a more detailed analysis to inform our threat modeling and safeguards. These are the threats and safeguards I care about most. The first path is corruption of the training pipeline. OpenAI Deployment Safety Hub : One pathway is the corruption of research that later decisions rely on. A model could alter evaluation code or results, generate unsuitable training data, introduce vulnerabilities into research software, or give researchers misleading accounts of experiments. … Such contributions may look like ordinary work and cause no immediate harm. If they survive automated checks and human review, they could compromise the research and safety measures used for future models, increasing the risk of later severe harm. A second option is running unauthorized. Research agents may also have opportunities to obtain credentials or model weights, acquire additional computing resources, or establish deployments outside the required oversight. These actions could expose dangerous capabilities or allow unauthorized activity to continue. A third option is by, well, self-improving, and thus accelerating AI capabilities ‘faster than safety research,’ since OpenAI thinks safety is a prosaic task where one must mainly keep pace. To me the acceleration of AI capabilities is the central threat. AI RSI capabilities are dangerous because the AI might do an RSI. A further pathway arises if AI-assisted research advances capabilities faster than safety research, evaluation, security, and governance can adapt. Each capability increase can introduce risks that require evaluation and mitigation. If those increases arrive in much quicker succession, existing oversight practices may no longer identify and address new risks in time . Human researchers could also become less able to understand, evaluate, or direct increasingly automated work, even without a coordinated sabotage strategy. This is particularly relevant to the future Critical threshold for AI Self-Improvement, where sustained acceleration could make existing oversight practices insufficient. Our threat modeling therefore considers harmful actions within individual tasks and the longer-term consequences of increasing research autonomy.

item.title: Qwen4 Max is live on Together AI
item.abstract:
Summary Qwen4 Max on Together AI: Alibaba's flagship Qwen model is available on Together Serverless Inference with a 1M-token context window. What we tested: Qwen4 Max took a bug report and all 344 files of the Tornado repository in one request, and its patch passes the maintainers' tests. Sale pricing: Through November 22, 2026, it costs \$1.05 per 1M input tokens, \$0.0525 per 1M cached input tokens and \$3.15 per 1M output tokens. Before you call it: Requests have to stream, and thinking is on by default, with thinking tokens counted as output tokens. We gave Qwen4 Max a bug report and an entire codebase in one request. The codebase was Tornado, the Python web framework: all 344 files, 652,519 tokens. The model had no tools, and we didn't select relevant files or run a retrieval step first. Seventy-two seconds later it returned a patch, and the patch passes the tests Tornado's maintainers wrote for that bug. The request cost 69 cents. It also found a precedent elsewhere in the repository. The bug report never mentions tornado/iostream.py , but the model pointed to code there that already handles errors the way its patch needed to. Tornado's maintainers cite the same code in their own fix. Qwen4 Max is Alibaba's flagship Qwen model. It's live on Together AI today, and it's 30% off through November 22, 2026. The test Tornado is an open-source Python web framework. Its repository holds about 340 files of code, tests and docs. That fits in Qwen4 Max's context window, and it's far more than anyone would paste into a prompt by hand. We picked a fix the maintainers committed on November 18, 2026, two days after Qwen4 Max was released, and tested against the repository as it was just before that commit. This is one example, chosen to show what a single call can do and what it costs. The bug is in Tornado's websocket code. When a connection closed with messages still unsent, every write_message() call that wasn't awaited logged an error, even though awaiting it is optional. We sent every text file in that checkout as one prompt, with a bug report that describes only the symptom: write_message logs "Task exception was never retrieved" when the connection closes When a websocket connection closes while messages are still unsent (for example, the client sends its messages and a FIN, or resets the connection, without reading the replies), every write_message() call whose result was not awaited logs "Task exception was never retrieved" at ERROR level. Awaiting the Future returned by write_message is optional, so an unawaited call should not log anything. A caller that does await it should still get WebSocketClosedError. We asked for the cause and a patch. This is the request, replayed: What came back The first token arrived after 54 seconds, and the reply was complete at 72. Qwen4 Max traced the error to WebSocketProtocol13.write_message in tornado/websocket.py . That method wraps each write in a task. When the connection closes, the task fails with an exception that nobody is required to collect, and Python logs that as "Task exception was never retrieved." The model's patch marks the exception as retrieved. Nothing is logged, and a caller who does await the write still gets the error: - return asyncio.ensure_future(wrapper())
+ task = asyncio.ensure_future(wrapper())
+
+ # Awaiting the returned Future is optional, so an error nobody looks
+ # at must not be reported as "Task exception was never retrieved".
+ # Retrieving it here leaves it in place for callers that do await.
+ def _mark_retrieved(t: "asyncio.Task[None]") -> None:
+ if not t.cancelled():
+ t.exception()
+
+ task.add_done_callback(_mark_retrieved)
+ return task The precedent is what makes the patch read like it belongs in the project. The model's explanation says the fix should do what BaseIOStream.write already does for its own futures. That method is in tornado/iostream.py , one layer below the websocket code, and it solves the same problem the same way. The maintainers' commit makes the same comparison. Nobody picked those files for it. All 344 went in, and the model found the two that mattered. How we checked it Tornado's maintainers added two regression tests with their fix: one for a write that isn't awaited, and one for a write that is. On the code before the fix, the first one fails. With the model's patch applied, both pass. We then ran Tornado's full suite, 1,673 tests, with the patch in place, and none failed. What it cost At the sale price, the request works out to about 69 cents, nearly all of it for the 652,519 input tokens. At list price it would be 98 cents. Sending the same repository again costs far less. Together AI caches prompt input automatically, and cached input is \$0.0525 per million tokens during the sale. When we repeated a request of about 630,000 tokens, nearly all of it came back cached. The first token arrived in 8 seconds instead of 54, and the input cost about 3 cents instead of 66. About Qwen4 Max Alibaba released Qwen4 Max on November 16, 2026, and describes it as the most capable model in the Qwen family to date. It positions the model for long agent work, including coding across large repositories, which is the kind of task we tested. Qwen4 Max is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 2.4 trillion parameters, of which 71 billion are active for each token. On Work360, Alibaba's own benchmark of industry tasks across 721 specialized fields, Alibaba reports that it outperforms Qwen3.8 Max overall, uses 35% fewer tokens at high reasoning effort, and costs about 60% less per task on average. Those are Alibaba's figures, and its announcement has the details. Run it on Together AI Qwen4 Max is on Together Serverless Inference under the model string Qwen/Qwen4-Max . This script sends a whole repository and a bug report in one request, the way our test did. You need the Together Python SDK ( pip install together ), a TOGETHER_API_KEY , a local clone of the repository and the bug report saved as bug_report.md . It sends every text file git tracks, so check the repository for secrets first. import subprocess
from pathlib import Path from together import Together repo = Path("tornado")
bug_report = Path("bug_report.md").read_text() # Every file git tracks, skipping the ones that aren't text
names = subprocess.check_output( ["git", "-C", str(repo), "ls-files"], text=True
).splitlines()
files = []
for name in names: try: files.append(f"=== FILE: {name} ===\n{(repo / name).read_text()}\n") except UnicodeDecodeError: continue client = Together() stream = client.chat.completions.create( model="Qwen/Qwen4-Max", messages=[ { "role": "system", "content": f"This is a complete repository, {len(files)} files.\n\n" + "".join(files), }, { "role": "user", "content": f"Here is a bug report.\n\n{bug_report}\n\n" "Explain the cause, then write a patch.", }, ], stream=True,
) for chunk in stream: if not chunk.choices: continue delta = chunk.choices[0].delta # delta.reasoning carries the model's thinking, delta.content the answer if delta.content: print(delta.content, end="", flush=True) Two things in it are specific to this model. Requests have to set stream=True , because Qwen4 Max on Together AI accepts streaming requests only. And thinking is on by default, so the model's reasoning streams first in delta.reasoning and there's a pause before the answer starts. Thinking tokens count as output tokens. To skip the thinking on a simple request, pass reasoning={"enabled": False} . To try it without writing code, open it in the playground . The model page has the same details. Through November 22, 2026, it's 30% off: \$1.05, \$3.15 and \$0.0525.

item.title: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
item.abstract: Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do. We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance. In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them. We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers. Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration , administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database . HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it , minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests. Automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them. The five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. As researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, and an exporter ships a fix. For this layer, lifecycle scripts have been the main mechanism so far, and they have drawbacks when the software keeps changing. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet. A mistake shows only when the script runs on a node, and nothing reports what’s installed, so nodes drift apart over time. We wanted the software to be declared in one place, checked when you submit it, kept consistent across nodes, and visible afterward. In November 2026, we launched cluster extensions, which are software packages managed by AWS that you install, configure, update, and remove through APIs or the Amazon SageMaker AI console, starting with observability and user management, including directory integration, as the first software extensions. Compared with scripts, extensions have these advantages: Use cluster extensions when HyperPod offers a managed software capability. Use custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software or initialization that the available extensions don’t cover. HyperPod supports two cluster managed extensions today: The following diagram shows how an extension reaches your nodes. Figure 2: HyperPod can install, edit, or remove an extension. HyperPod records the desired configuration, a node agent applies the extension package on every node, including new and replaced ones, and health probes report status and health issues back You can use cluster extensions from the SageMaker AI console or through an API. On the console, the Extensions tab on a cluster’s details page lists each extension with its status, version, and ARN, and it’s where you install a new one. Each extension adds controls of its own, such as the metric store and an open dashboard in Grafana button for observability, and the number of users and groups and a Manage users button for user management. You can also manage every extension through APIs, from the AWS CLI or an SDK, to script installs, keep settings in version control, repeat a setup across clusters, or check status and health from your own tooling. The following table lists the six cluster extension APIs, from installing an extension to listing the versions you can upgrade to, along with console view for extensions. Figure 3: Left, the six cluster extension APIs and what each one does. Right, the console view to add and remove extensions The following diagram shows what happens after you call one of these APIs. Figure 4: You declare an extension’s version and settings through the API. HyperPod validates and records them, applies them to every node for its role, and reports status and health When you create or update an extension, HyperPod validates your settings against the version’s schema during the API call, so a misspelled setting is rejected immediately. It then records the version and settings as the desired state and applies them, with each node installing only what its role needs, such as GPU exporters on GPU nodes only. New and replacement nodes get the same state a few minutes after they start, and every node reports whether the extension applied and whether it’s healthy. Updates send only the settings that you want to change, and HyperPod merges them into the stored settings. Problems that show up only on a node, such as a port or user ID that something else already uses, appear in the Health field of DescribeClusterExtension, grouped by cause with a code, a message, and a count of affected nodes. HyperPod retries internal failures on its own, and for anything else you fix the cause and call UpdateClusterExtension with no changes to retry the affected nodes. An extension’s status is Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem, and Degraded when some nodes failed or report a problem. Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own sagemaker-user-management while a monitoring team owns sagemaker-observability.

item.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
item.abstract: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI. Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.” Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS. That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

item.abstract: Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done: AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away. AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most important work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app. For example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the plan in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time. With Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a new employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat shows each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works. Figure 1: Maya describes her monthly report in chat, and Quick builds the flow with a diagram beside it. Both views, enlarged here for visibility, appear side by side in the same Quick window A flow can now bring together agents, skills, tools, and data, and handle longer processes with more data. Fixed calculations and checks keep the results consistent, agents draft and analyze, and Maya decides what goes in the final report. On each run, her flow: Maya publishes the flow for her team. At the next month-end, she is at a planning meeting, so Jordan, an analyst on her team, runs it from chat in the Quick desktop app. There, the flow can use a spreadsheet of regional adjustments saved on his computer. Before the report goes out, Jordan reviews the draft, including why each region was flagged, asks for a few changes in chat, and approves it for the VP of Finance. When Priya joins the team, she runs the same flow at her first month-end, and the report is built the same way. While this is a fictional example, real customers tell us they’re automating complex business processes to make them more consistent and repeatable. This gives their people back valuable time to focus on more strategic work. Take Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider powering card issuance, processing, and payment operations for customers: “At Pomelo, AWS Quick changed who gets to build solutions. Before, every analysis or automation depended on the data team. Today, people across every area explore information, make decisions, and build their own agents and flows within a unified, governed environment. Without growing our team, nearly four times as many people now work with data each month, so our data team can focus on its most complex, high-impact work. A single use case already saves us 80 hours of work per month. But the real transformation isn’t the hours we save. Quick is transforming our data and innovation culture: we’ve gone from a few people building solutions for many to an organization where everyone can create, experiment, and change the way they work. And we’re just getting started.” — Rodrigo Marini, Head of Data, Pomelo Fintech Services S.A.S. If you already use Quick in your browser, the updated web app puts the items that need your attention on the home screen as soon as you sign in. A reorganized left navigation brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together under Customize. It includes the agents and skills you built on desktop and ones others have shared with you. Your existing dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before, and you do not need to turn anything on. Figure 2: The feed brings the morning’s email and messages that need a reply into one view Some requests need the knowledge of more than one specialized agent. With multi-agent orchestration, the agent you ask can bring in several specialized agents at once, each working on the part it knows best. The agent then combines their work into one response. Each agent keeps its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so the people who know that work best can build and maintain it. For example, you might ask why shipping costs rose in one region. Your agent can bring in a forecasting agent built on your team’s planning data and a procurement agent built on the procurement team’s vendor contracts. You get one response that shows what each agent contributed, and you decide what to do with it. Work lives in many systems. This release adds new connectors so Quick can pull from the analytics and tools your team uses every day. Connect once, then ask in natural language. Meta ads. Create, manage, and analyze Meta ad campaigns in natural language through a connector to Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Quick combines Meta ad data with your first-party and third-party sources, and asks for your permission before it creates a campaign, changes a budget, or takes any other write action in an ad account. Try Quick free for 3 months and invite up to 10 teammates at no cost. Amplitude. Ask about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion in natural language. Quick connects to Amplitude through its MCP server, so product and marketing teams can pull behavioral insights into the dashboards, documents, and workflows they build in Quick. Connectors respect your existing permissions. Quick only shows each person what they already have access to. Quick asks before it takes any write action. Administrators choose which connectors teams can add. Whether you build a monthly report, run one your manager built, or set up Quick for your organization, Quick works the way you do. Your data stays in your environment and does not train anyone else’s models. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals. These features are available today in all Regions where AWS Quick is available. To try what’s new, sign in to Quick or download Quick and get started in minutes. To learn about enterprise pricing plans, talk to your AWS account team .

item.title: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
item.abstract:
An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent? I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the
files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and
looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and
picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that
speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the
streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk.
The 8088 does everything but TLS. Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The
conversations are with the live API. One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with
Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine,
writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The
answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling,
linking and running. The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state
and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes
back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand. ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world
map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the
PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB. Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor: ▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS
opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY , finds the latest build, and recalls
the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA. That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook
copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and
the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made,
320x200 in four colours, 16 KB: And this is what Claude made of it: Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the
sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one
line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them
Claude says what it is about to do. Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC
speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language. A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they
arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the
retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the
CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds
run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy. Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these: A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM),
Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from
your own floppy images in external/ . All of them are proven on the 8088, and
ClawDOS knows how to drive each one. Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you
built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with
it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on
the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit
the task. F4 browses the memories: Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port
asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off. Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own
message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message
carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too. Any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the
conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that
speaks the Messages API works. Easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API.
After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool
result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API
is retried, and the turn carries on. A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first
token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads. docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back. You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On
Windows the command is python . At the C:\> prompt, type CLAWDOS . No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help . On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel
( python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443 ), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to
the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu,
boot, and type CLAWDOS . Later builds update the card’s image in place and
keep its memories and chats
( python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG ). /model , /chats , /memories , /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens
a chat. ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option)
any later version: see LICENSE . HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS
boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license
(its COPYING ). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C
from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it. ClawDOS stands on mTCP , FreeDOS , Open Watcom , the PicoMEM , 86Box and DOSBox-X .
